A narrow, 3.5 km-wide strait called Uzun-Aral divides the lake into two chemically distinct basins. The western half is relatively shallow and consists of nearly fresh water, thanks to the massive inflow from the Ili River. In contrast, the eastern half is significantly deeper and remarkably salty, as it lacks major freshwater sources and loses water rapidly to evaporation. This hydrological "Jekyll and Hyde" personality makes it one of the most unique large-scale water bodies on the planet.
Trivia:
Because it is an endorheic basin, water flows in but never flows out to an ocean; it simply evaporates or soaks into the ground.
The lake is currently facing a "mini-Aral Sea" crisis; as water is diverted for irrigation upstream in China and Kazakhstan, the lake is shrinking and the freshwater western side is becoming increasingly saline.

7. In strictly geological terms, it meets every criterion: a distinct crustal landmass, a defined tectonic boundary, its own geological identity separate from the continent beside it. And yet for centuries it went uncatalogued — because 94% of it lies beneath the ocean. Only a sparse scattering of islands remain above the surface, the last visible remnants of a landmass that once stood proud above the waves before gradually subsiding. The concept of it as a continent was first formally proposed in 1995 and has gained substantial scientific recognition since, though it remains absent from most school textbooks and atlases.
